Preprint · October 2026

Latency-Native Media: Designing Shared Experience for an Interplanetary Civilization

Abhiram Nimmala

October 17, 2026

Abstract

Almost everything we share with other people assumes the other person is with us in the same moment. A phone call, a group chat during a game, a watch party: all of them depend on replies that arrive within seconds. On Mars, a signal to Earth takes between about 3 and 22 minutes, and no improvement in technology will shorten that, because the limit is the speed of light. Space agencies have studied communication delay for decades, but mostly as a problem of mission operations. Much less is known about how people who live inside that delay will stay close to the family, friends and culture they left behind.

In this paper I treat interplanetary delay as a media design problem. I first build a quantitative model of delayed interaction. At the average Mars delay, two people can exchange fewer than five messages an hour, and the gap between Mars delay and the tolerance of ordinary conversation spans three to four orders of magnitude. Once realistic schedules and the 40-minute daily drift between Martian and Earth days are included, a settler may get only about two live conversational turns a day with someone on Earth, against hundreds for two people in the same time zone. I then propose four latency-native design strategies (asynchronous co-watching, predictive avatars, batched conversation and ghost multiplayer) that are built around delay rather than patched to survive it. Finally, I test three of them in an agent-based simulation: 2,800 runs covering 1,400 simulated pairs under each design, across Earth, Moon and Mars conditions and a full Earth–Mars orbital cycle. At the average Mars delay, ordinary real-time habits make conversations about 6.5 times slower than on Earth and eliminate two-way shared moments entirely. Latency-native designs cut conversation time in half and restore two-way sharing for 57% of events, although the conversation result depends heavily on whether question tracking works in practice. Schedule drift and light delay turn out to compound, and each one alone roughly triples conversation time. I close with design principles for the media of an interplanetary civilization and with uses on Earth today, from polar research stations to communities with poor connectivity.

Keywords: communication delay, human-computer interaction, social presence, Mars, space habitation, asynchronous media, computational media

1. Introduction

1.1 A championship game, 22 minutes late

Picture a settler at a research base on Mars sometime in the 2040s. Back home in Georgia, her younger brother is playing in a championship basketball game. Her family is crowded around the television. Her parents argue with the referees, her cousins trade jokes in the group chat, and when her brother hits the winning shot, everyone in the room shouts at once. It lasts a few seconds, and nobody misses it.

She can watch the same broadcast from Mars, but it reaches her up to 22 minutes late. By the time she sees the ball leave her brother's hands, her family has already celebrated, posted the clip and moved on to arguing about the next round. She records her reaction and sends it home. Twenty-two minutes later it lands in a chat that has gone quiet. A few people reply politely. No one shouts with her.

Every bit of data reached her. She was, technically, connected to everyone she loves. In the way that mattered that evening, she was alone.

This paper is about the distance between being connected and feeling together. My argument is that this distance will be one of the defining human problems of living beyond Earth, that engineering cannot close it, and that careful design can narrow it.

1.2 Why better engineering will not fix this

Most communication problems have eventually yielded to faster or bigger systems. Copper phone lines gave way to fiber, grainy video to 4K, and half-second satellite delays to low-orbit constellations measured in tens of milliseconds. It would be natural to expect interplanetary links to follow the same path.

For bandwidth, they will. Laser communication is already raising the data rates possible from deep space, and future Mars links may well carry high-definition video. Latency is a separate matter. Bandwidth describes how much data arrives per second; latency describes how long the first bit takes to arrive at all. A wider pipe carries more water, but the water does not get there any sooner.

Interplanetary latency rests on two facts that no technology can change: nothing travels faster than light, and Mars is far away. The distance between the two planets swings from about 55 million to more than 400 million kilometres as they orbit the Sun, which gives a one-way delay of roughly 3 to 22 minutes (Chapter 2). No radio, protocol or routing scheme can beat that. Anyone who lives on Mars will live with it for good.

That makes interplanetary delay an unusual kind of engineering problem. It is not waiting for a breakthrough. It is a permanent feature of the environment, as fixed as Martian gravity or the length of a Martian day, and the sensible response is the same one we give to gravity: design around it.

1.3 What existing research covers, and what it leaves out

Space agencies have taken communication delay seriously for a long time. In the best-known study, Mars-500, six men lived sealed inside modules in Moscow for 520 days while every written message to the outside world was artificially delayed [3], [4]. NASA's Human Exploration Research Analog (HERA) runs 45-day missions with delayed communication [6], its NEEMO missions have carried out undersea science dives under a 15-minute delay [7], and one study imposed 50-second delays on real astronauts aboard the International Space Station [8]. A recent NASA review collected 117 papers on the subject [10].

Nearly all of this work asks the same question: how can a crew and its mission control get work done when they cannot talk in real time? The outcomes it measures are operational, such as whether tasks are completed correctly, how quickly anomalies are resolved and how much autonomy a crew needs. For early missions, where survival comes first, that is the right focus.

The first permanent settlers, though, will not only be crew members. They will have parents, siblings, partners, friends and children on another planet. They will want to celebrate birthdays, follow their teams, argue about politics and feel part of a culture that mostly happens somewhere else. ESA has said plainly that crews unable to maintain meaningful connections with loved ones may face health consequences from prolonged isolation, and that the wider consequences of delay have received little research [1].

Put simply, there is a well-developed science of delayed coordination and almost no science of delayed connection. This paper is an attempt to start one.

1.4 Research questions

The main question is this: what forms of shared media and interaction can keep people socially connected when every message between them takes minutes to arrive? I approach it through three narrower questions.

  1. RQ1 (Characterization). How, and how quickly, do engagement and the sense of being together break down as one-way delay grows from zero to more than 20 minutes?
  2. RQ2 (Design). Which design strategies, such as asynchronous co-watching, predictive replies, batched conversation and ghost-based play, recover the most of what is lost?
  3. RQ3 (Generalization). Can these strategies be turned into general principles for latency-native media, meaning media designed for delay from the start?

1.5 Thesis

I argue that delay should be treated as a design material, not a defect. Today's media treat delay as a flaw to minimize; a video call with a two-second lag is simply a bad call. That view works when delay can be reduced. It breaks down when delay is permanent and measured in minutes, because media that try to stay real-time across interplanetary distances will feel broken forever.

The alternative is media whose experience is built on delay instead of damaged by it. A letter is not a failed phone call; it is a different and valuable way of communicating. I call this kind of design latency-native media, and I propose that it can preserve a real sense of togetherness where real-time media cannot.

1.6 Contributions

The paper makes four contributions:

  1. A quantitative model of delayed interaction (Chapter 4), which shows how delay limits conversational turns, how long ordinary exchanges take, and how schedules and blackouts make matters worse. It introduces the synchrony gap, a single number that expresses how far a given delay sits from the limits of natural conversation.
  2. A taxonomy of media by synchrony dependence (Chapter 4), which sorts experiences into four levels by what is lost when the other person is not present at the same moment, and shows which ones fail first.
  3. Four latency-native design strategies (Chapter 5) for shared viewing, conversation and play.
  4. An agent-based delay simulator and simulation study (Chapters 6 and 7) that tests these strategies across Earth, Moon and Mars conditions and a full orbital cycle, checked against the analytic model, together with a ready-to-run design for a human study (Appendix E).

1.7 Scope

The focus here is social communication between individuals and small groups: families, friends and communities. Mission-critical operations are already well covered by existing research, and the engineering of the data link is the job of delay-tolerant networking (Chapter 2). I use Mars as the main case because it is the most likely site of permanent settlement in the coming decades and because its delay is long enough to break real-time media completely. The Moon serves as an intermediate case, and much of the argument applies on Earth wherever latency, schedules or poor connectivity keep people apart.

1.8 How the paper is organized

Chapter 2 covers the physics of interplanetary delay, what is known about the timing of human conversation, and what analog missions have learned. Chapter 3 reviews related work in spaceflight research, communication theory, asynchronous media and games, and identifies the gap. Chapter 4 presents the model and taxonomy, and Chapter 5 the four design strategies. Chapter 6 describes the simulation and Chapter 7 its results. Chapter 8 discusses what the results mean, Chapter 9 looks at future applications, and Chapter 10 concludes.

2. Background

The rest of the paper rests on a handful of facts about physics and about people. I start with where interplanetary delay comes from and how it changes over time (2.1), then add two further timing effects that make it worse (2.2). After that I turn to human conversation and how finely it is timed (2.3), to the engineering and human-factors work already done on delay (2.4 and 2.5), and finally to social presence, the concept I use to talk about connection (2.6).

2.1 The physics of interplanetary delay

The one-way delay D between two points is their distance d divided by the speed of light c:

Solar-system distances are usually measured in astronomical units (AU), the average distance from Earth to the Sun. Light crosses one AU in 499.0 seconds, or 8.317 minutes, so:

The Moon, about 384,400 km away, is 1.3 light-seconds from Earth. For Mars the answer depends on where both planets sit in their orbits.

Earth circles the Sun at about 1.0 AU once a year. Mars circles at about 1.52 AU, on a noticeably elliptical path, once every 687 days. Because Earth moves faster, it keeps catching up with Mars and then pulling ahead. The planets are closest around opposition, when Earth passes between Mars and the Sun, and farthest around conjunction, when the Sun lies between them. One full cycle, the synodic period, takes about 780 days, a little over two years.

Mars's elongated orbit means that close approaches are not all equally close. An opposition that falls near Mars's perihelion brings the planets unusually near each other; one near aphelion leaves them relatively far apart even at their closest. The minimum delay therefore changes from one cycle to the next.

To see how this plays out over the period when crewed missions are being planned, I computed the Earth–Mars distance for every day from January 2026 to December 2035, using standard J2000 mean orbital elements and solving Kepler's equation numerically for each planet's position (Appendix A). The model ignores the 1.85° tilt of Mars's orbit, which costs about ±0.3 minutes of accuracy. Figure 1 shows the result.

Over the decade, the one-way delay runs from 3.2 minutes (September 2035, a favourable perihelic opposition) to 22.3 minutes (August 2034, near conjunction), with an average of 13.9 minutes. The low points are uneven: the close approaches of 2027 and 2029 never drop below 5 minutes, while those of 2033 and 2035 approach 3. These figures agree with ESA's published range of roughly 3.5 to just over 22 minutes [1], and with Mars Express operators' description of round-trip times from about 8 minutes to nearly an hour.

Light travel time is only the floor. Real systems add delay for encoding, error correction, relaying through orbiters and queuing. ESA notes that although the Moon is 1.3 light-seconds away, digital processing in Artemis-era systems could push lunar delay as high as 10 seconds one way [1]; the Apollo crews, using analog radio, never had that overhead. Future Mars links will add their own processing time on top of the 3 to 22 minutes set by physics.

Two points matter most for design. The delay is never small: even at the best alignment, a question and its answer are more than six minutes apart. And it is never constant. It shifts every day and varies by a factor of seven across two years, so any system that assumes a fixed delay will be wrong most of the time.

2.2 Blackouts and drifting days

About once every 26 months, Mars passes almost directly behind the Sun as seen from Earth. Near that point, radio signals have to cross the Sun's hot, turbulent outer atmosphere, which scrambles them, and mission controllers routinely stop commanding Mars spacecraft for roughly two weeks. For a settlement, this means that every two years or so, contact with Earth may be partly or completely cut for about two weeks, and the cut comes exactly when delay is already at its longest.

The second effect is quieter. A Martian solar day, or sol, lasts 24 hours, 39 minutes and 35 seconds, about 40 minutes longer than a day on Earth. Settlers will almost certainly live on Mars time, since sunlight governs their power, their temperature and their circadian rhythms. Their clock will therefore drift against Earth's by about 40 minutes a day. In roughly 36 days the drift adds up to a full day, and a settler's morning slides through every hour of the Earth day before coming back around.

The practical consequence is that the hours when someone on Mars and someone on Earth are both awake and free keep moving. One week a settler's evening may line up with her family's evening; a few weeks later it falls in the middle of their night. Any model of delayed conversation that assumes both people are always available will overstate how much contact is possible, a point I return to in Chapter 4.

2.3 How finely timed conversation is

To see why minutes of delay do so much damage, it helps to know how tightly normal conversation is timed.

Turn-taking is fast. A cross-cultural study of conversation in ten languages, ranging from Japanese and Danish to the Mayan language Tzeltal, found that speakers in all of them avoid both overlapping talk and long silences, and that the typical gap between one person finishing and the next starting is around 200 milliseconds [14]. Planning even a short reply takes longer than that, so listeners must be predicting where the other person's turn will end and preparing an answer before it does. Conversation is tightly coordinated and largely predictive.

Because the expected gap is so short, longer pauses get noticed and read for meaning. A slow answer to an invitation is often heard as reluctance or as a polite "no." Under delay, people may read intentions into silences that are caused purely by physics.

Conversation also depends on what researchers call grounding: partners keep signalling to each other that they have understood, through small acknowledgements, nods and follow-up questions, and in doing so build a shared base of understanding [20]. Grounding needs fast feedback. When feedback takes minutes, misunderstandings go uncorrected and neither side can easily check that they are on the same page.

Telephone engineering has put numbers on these limits. ITU-T Recommendation G.114 states that most applications are not significantly affected when one-way delay stays below 150 milliseconds, and it recommends 400 milliseconds as the upper limit for general network planning [2]. Beyond that, people start talking over each other, hesitating and losing the rhythm of the exchange. Figure 2 puts interplanetary delays on the same scale.

The contrast is stark. The 1.3-second lunar delay is already more than three times the G.114 planning limit, enough to make ordinary back-and-forth noticeably awkward. The shortest Mars delay, 3.2 minutes, is about 1,300 times the 150-millisecond threshold, and the longest is nearly 9,000 times it. A call to Mars is not a degraded phone call; it is a different kind of communication altogether.

2.4 Delay-tolerant networking

On the engineering side, moving data across long and unreliable links is largely a solved problem. The Internet's core protocols assume an unbroken end-to-end path and short round trips, and they fail when either assumption does. Delay-tolerant networking (DTN) was developed for exactly those conditions. Its central protocol, now standardized as Bundle Protocol version 7 [19], works on a store-and-forward basis: each node holds data until the next link opens and then passes it on, so that data can cross a path that is never fully connected at any single moment.

DTN gets the bytes across. It does not decide what those bytes should mean to the person receiving them. A DTN link can deliver a video call to Mars without dropping a frame, but it cannot make that call feel like a conversation. This paper therefore works one layer above DTN, at the level of human experience. It assumes reliable delivery and asks what is worth delivering.

2.5 What analog missions have learned

No one has yet lived with minutes of delay, so the best evidence comes from analog missions: long simulations on Earth that reproduce selected features of deep-space life.

The most ambitious of these, Mars-500, sealed an international crew of six men (three Russian, two European and one Chinese) inside a 550-cubic-metre facility at the Institute of Biomedical Problems in Moscow for 520 days, roughly the length of a real round trip [3], [4]. The mission script covered the outbound flight, a simulated landing and surface work, and the return. From day 35 to day 490, telephone contact was removed, and every written message in either direction, email included, passed through software that imposed a delay growing with the simulated distance from Earth [3]. Both the crew and mission control came to regard video messages as the most effective channel during that period, partly because video gave the crew a way to express negative emotions [3]. The mission's psychological support team studied the crew's private communication with the outside world and concluded that, once real-time contact is gone, contact with home becomes a vital part of psychological support [4]. Midway through, the crew also lived through a week-long simulated total blackout, a preview of solar conjunction.

A later study compared crew communication in Mars-500 with SIRIUS-19, which had a mixed-gender crew and a 5-minute delay [5]. Both missions showed signs of a psychological "detachment" effect, in which isolation, autonomy and delay changed how crews communicated with mission control, and both showed a temporary rise in communication around the simulated landing. The authors concluded that the results confirmed concerns about the effect of delay on the quality of information exchange [5].

NASA's Human Exploration Research Analog is a two-storey, 650-square-foot habitat at Johnson Space Center that houses four-person crews for up to 45 days. Studies there have used delay to examine crew autonomy, including whether crews can and will plan their own work with a scheduling tool called Playbook [6]. During NEEMO 21, aquanauts in an undersea habitat carried out science and exploration dives under a 15-minute delay to develop tools and procedures for Mars [7]. And aboard the International Space Station, astronauts performed selected tasks with a 50-second one-way delay, with the reported effects showing up mainly in off-nominal situations [8].

Taken together, these missions show that delay can be lived with, that it degrades communication, that it can produce psychological detachment, and that richer media such as video help. They also show where the field's attention has gone. Almost every measured outcome concerns crews and mission control working together. Personal communication appears mostly as a support service to be provided, rarely as a design problem in its own right.

2.6 Social presence

To study connection, I need some way of describing and measuring it. I use the idea of social presence, which comes from research on telecommunication in the 1970s. Short, Williams and Christie proposed that media differ in how strongly they convey the presence of the other person, and that this quality shapes how people use them [17]. A face-to-face meeting conveys a lot of social presence; a business letter conveys very little.

Later work broke the idea into measurable parts. The Networked Minds measure developed by Biocca and Harms treats social presence as the sense of being together with another person in a mediated environment [9], made up of several dimensions:

  • Co-presence: the feeling of not being alone, of sharing a space with the other person.
  • Attentional allocation: how much attention each person gives to, and feels from, the other.
  • Perceived message understanding: whether each person feels they understand the other and are understood in return.
  • Perceived affective and behavioral interdependence: whether each person's emotions and actions seem to affect, and be affected by, the other's.

In validation testing, the measure distinguished face-to-face interaction from mediated interaction and told different levels of mediated interaction apart [9]. That makes it a good fit for the question here: whether a delayed experience can still feel shared, and whether some designs feel more shared than others.

3. Related Work

Five bodies of work bear on this problem, each from a different direction: spaceflight research on communication delay, theories of computer-mediated communication, the long history of asynchronous media, latency techniques from online games, and the newer field of AI-mediated communication. I review each in turn and then bring them together to locate the gap.

3.1 Communication delay in spaceflight research

NASA's Human Research Program treats communication delay as a contributor to one of its formal risks: the risk of poor performance and adverse outcomes caused by inadequate cooperation, coordination, communication and psychosocial adaptation within a team. As part of understanding that risk, NASA researchers recently carried out the first in-depth systematic review of the delay literature since 2013, gathering 117 papers that used terms such as "communication delay" and "communication latency" [10].

The review's overall picture matches the analog missions in Chapter 2. As delay grows, communication between crew and ground degrades, and team performance and cohesion can suffer [10]. The evidence is not uniformly bleak. One study summarized by NASA found that a 2.5-second one-way delay did not affect performance on its task, though the authors cautioned that longer delays could [11]. Crews working under delay have reported that it changed how they asserted themselves within the team, and high crew autonomy has generally been well received, although its effects are hard to separate from those of the delay itself [11].

The countermeasures follow naturally from this framing. If delay makes it harder for mission control to direct a crew, the answer is to shift responsibility to the crew: better onboard procedures, decision-support tools and self-scheduling software [6], [10]. These are sensible answers to an operational problem.

What this literature does not study is just as telling. Its outcome measures are task performance, workload, scheduling and coordination. Its participants are crews talking to mission controllers in professional roles. Personal and family communication appears, if at all, as a background support measure. I found no study in this body of work that designs or compares media specifically to preserve personal connection under interplanetary delay.

3.2 Theories of computer-mediated communication

Communication researchers have spent decades studying how media shape relationships, and three ideas are especially useful here.

The first is social presence theory, described in Chapter 2: Short, Williams and Christie's argument that media differ in how much they convey the presence of the other person [17]. Early versions of the theory predicted that low-presence media such as text would be poorly suited to warm, personal communication. My measures come from this tradition.

The second is media richness theory. Daft and Lengel proposed that media vary in richness, meaning their capacity to carry multiple cues such as voice, facial expression and gesture, to give immediate feedback, to use natural language and to convey personal focus [15]. Face-to-face talk is the richest medium and a written memo among the leanest, and they argued that rich media suit ambiguous or emotional messages while lean media suit simple, factual ones. One of their four criteria, immediate feedback, is precisely what interplanetary delay removes. A video message from Mars keeps voice, face and gesture but loses feedback, so it no longer sits neatly on their scale. That suggests delay is a separate dimension from richness, and that latency-native design can aim for as much richness as possible while accepting that immediate feedback is gone.

The third idea offers some reassurance. Not every study found that lean, slow media harm relationships. Walther observed that people who communicate through text often build relationships as warm as face-to-face ones, given enough time, and sometimes more intimate ones [16]. His explanation was that asynchronous media give senders time to compose and present themselves with care, and give receivers room to fill gaps with generous impressions. For this paper that is an important source of optimism: delay does not automatically destroy connection. What matters is whether the medium lets people use the extra time well.

3.3 A long history of asynchronous media

For most of history, people kept relationships going across long delays. Letters carried by ship took weeks or months to cross an ocean, yet emigrant families, soldiers and explorers maintained deep bonds through them. Early twentieth-century polar expeditions were cut off for months at a time. Correspondence chess, played by post, has run for centuries, with single moves taking days and games lasting years.

Much of today's communication is asynchronous too: email, voice notes, recorded video messages, long posts and shared photo albums. Even nominally real-time tools get used asynchronously, as anyone who has caught up on a group chat hours later knows.

All of this shows that delay and closeness can coexist. The Mars case differs in one crucial way, however. In the past, delay applied to everyone, and cultures built rituals and expectations around it. Today's asynchronous media sit inside a world where real-time contact is always available as a fallback. A settler on Mars will face the reverse: permanent delay for her, while everyone she knows on Earth carries on in real time. Her family will still watch games live, still expect instant replies from each other, still make plans in chats that move faster than she can follow. No existing asynchronous medium was designed for that mismatch.

3.4 Latency techniques in online games

Online multiplayer games face a small version of the same problem and have developed clever responses to it. Fast games need every action to feel instant, yet network delays of 50 to 200 milliseconds are common. Developers have handled this in several ways [18]:

  • Client-side prediction. Each player's device shows the result of their own actions immediately and predicts where other players will be, then corrects itself when the real data arrives.
  • Lag compensation. The server effectively rewinds the game to judge each action as it looked to the player who made it, so that a shot that hit on the shooter's screen counts as a hit.
  • Ghosts. Racing and puzzle games let players compete against recordings of other players' runs, so that competing does not require being online together.
  • Turn-based design. Strategy and word games let each player move whenever they are ready, sometimes days apart.

These techniques show that good design can hide, absorb or reframe delay, and client-side prediction directly inspired the predictive avatars in Chapter 5. All of them, though, were built for delays of milliseconds, or for games that were turn-based from the start. None has been tested as a way to keep people socially connected across minutes.

3.5 AI-mediated communication

A newer line of research looks at AI-mediated communication, in which an artificial intelligence modifies, augments or generates messages on someone's behalf [21]. Suggested replies in email, autocomplete and tools that rewrite a message to sound more polite or confident are all everyday examples. Researchers have raised concerns that such systems can change how people present themselves, alter how much recipients trust a message, and blur the line between what a person said and what a machine said for them [21].

This matters for interplanetary communication because large language models now make it plausible for software to write a reply in the style of a particular person. With minutes of silence to fill, the temptation to let a model do so will be strong. The predictive avatar strategy in Chapter 5 takes up this possibility on purpose, and Chapter 8 discusses its risks.

3.6 The gap

Table 1 summarizes where existing work sits relative to this paper.

Body of work Delay scale Main focus Social connection under permanent delay?

Delay-tolerant networking [19] Minutes to hours Reliable data delivery No
Telecom quality standards [2] Milliseconds Call quality No

Table 1. Positioning of this paper relative to existing research.

The table makes three things clear. The one field that studies interplanetary-scale delay, spaceflight research, does not study social connection. The fields that do study connection assume that real-time contact is there as a fallback. And the fields with the best techniques for hiding delay work at millisecond scales or do not address delay at all.

As far as I can tell, no previous work designs and tests media for social connection under permanent, interplanetary-scale delay, a gap that ESA itself has identified as an open research area [1]. This paper tries to begin filling it by combining the operational knowledge of spaceflight research, the relational insights of communication theory and the design techniques of games.

4. A Model of Delayed Interaction

In this chapter I build a simple quantitative model of how delay limits interaction. I begin with an idealized best case (4.2), then add the realities of availability and drifting days (4.3 and 4.4) and of blackouts (4.5), and condense the results into one comparative measure, the synchrony gap (4.6). Section 4.7 introduces a taxonomy of media by how much they depend on synchrony, and Section 4.8 sets out the predictions that Chapters 6 and 7 then test in simulation.

4.1 Assumptions and notation

The model describes two people, one on Earth and one on Mars, exchanging messages. Table 2 lists the notation.

Symbol Meaning Value used
D One-way signal delay 3.2, 13.9 or 22.3 min (Chapter 2)
T Time to read a message and write a reply 0.5 min
N Number of messages in an exchange 10
A Hours per day each person is free to talk 4 h
W Average wait for the recipient to be free derived below
τ Longest pause tolerated in live conversation 0.4 s (G.114 ceiling)

Table 2. Model notation.

I assume reliable delivery, which DTN handles (Chapter 2), and ignore processing delay, so every result here is a best case. Real systems will be slower.

4.2 The best case: both people waiting

Suppose both people are free, paying attention and waiting for each other. Each turn then costs the time for the message to travel plus the time to reply, D + T, so the maximum number of turns per hour is:

With T at half a minute, two people on Earth can manage about 120 turns an hour. At the closest Mars delay that falls to about 16, and at the decade-average delay of 13.9 minutes to about 4. A ten-message conversation that takes five minutes on Earth stretches to 2.4 hours at average delay and 3.8 hours at the maximum (Figure 3, Table 3).

Even the best case is severe. At average delay, two people who sat at their screens for an entire evening could swap about 17 messages, roughly what two friends on Earth manage in a few minutes of texting.

4.3 Adding availability

The best case assumes both people are waiting. In practice they work, sleep, eat and spend time with others. Suppose each person has a single free window of A hours a day. A message arriving at a random moment will usually find its recipient busy and must wait until the window opens. For one window of A hours in a 24-hour day, the average wait is:

With a four-hour window, W comes to about 8.3 hours. Each turn now costs D + T + W, and the delay itself almost disappears next to the waiting: a ten-message exchange takes about 3.5 days whether Mars is near or far.

This is one of the more useful things the model shows. Once people stop waiting at their screens, interplanetary conversation behaves like letter-writing, with roughly one exchange a day. Physical delay matters most in the rare moments when both people happen to be free at once.

4.4 Drifting days and shared windows

On Earth, two family members in the same time zone tend to be free at the same hours, often in the evening. On Mars, as Chapter 2 explained, the day is about 40 minutes longer. If the settler's free window follows Mars time and her family's follows Earth time, the two windows slide past each other by 40 minutes a day and return to the same alignment every 36 days.

I simulated this drift over a full 36-day cycle, with two four-hour windows and the requirement that the first message of a live exchange arrive while both people are still free. Table 4 shows the results.

Scenario Days per cycle with any usable overlap Live turns per day (cycle average)
Earth, same time zone 100% ~480
Mars, closest (3.2 min) 33% ~10
Mars, average (13.9 min) 31% ~2.3
Mars, farthest (22.3 min) 30% ~1.3

Table 4. Live (near-real-time) conversation turns available per day when two 4-hour free windows drift against each other by 40 minutes per day. Simulated over a 36-day cycle.

For about two-thirds of every cycle, the settler and her family are never free at the same time, so no live exchange can happen at all. When their windows do overlap, delay consumes most of the shared time. Averaged over the cycle, a settler at the average Mars delay gets about 2 live turns a day, compared with roughly 480 for two people in the same time zone on Earth, a reduction of around 200 times.

This changes how the problem should be framed. Interplanetary connection is limited not just by the speed of light but by delay, schedules and drifting days acting together. A design that only shortens the delay people perceive will not help much. A design that lets people share experiences outside their overlapping windows might.

4.5 Blackouts

So far the link has been assumed to be always on. Around each solar conjunction, roughly every 26 months, it may be degraded or cut for about two weeks (Chapter 2), and Mars-500 simulated a week-long total blackout [3]. During such periods, turns per day fall to zero. Because conjunction coincides with maximum delay, the weeks before a blackout are already the worst of the cycle for conversation. Latency-native media should therefore help people prepare, letting them record messages, reactions and content in advance for release while the link is down.

4.6 The synchrony gap

To compare delay directly with human tolerance, I define the synchrony gap G as the round-trip delay divided by the longest pause people will tolerate in live conversation:

Taking τ as 0.4 seconds, the G.114 planning ceiling [2], gives the values in Table 5.

Link One-way delay Synchrony gap G Interpretation
Same city ~5 ms ~0.03 Natural conversation
Intercontinental call ~150 ms ~0.75 Natural, slightly stiff
Earth–Moon (physics) 1.3 s ~6 Awkward; needs turn-taking etiquette
Earth–Moon (Artemis est.) up to 10 s ~50 Walkie-talkie style only
Earth–Mars, closest 3.2 min ~950 Real-time impossible
Earth–Mars, farthest 22.3 min ~6,700 Real-time impossible

Table 5. Synchrony gap for different links.

The values fall into three regimes. Below a gap of about 1, real-time media work with minor tuning. Between about 1 and 100, as on the Moon, conversation is still possible but needs explicit turn-taking, much like a walkie-talkie. In the hundreds or thousands, real-time media do not merely degrade; they stop working, and a different kind of medium is needed. Mars sits squarely in that third regime.

4.7 A taxonomy of synchrony dependence

Not every experience depends on synchrony to the same degree. I sort media into four levels according to what is lost when the other person is not present at the same moment (Table 6).

Level Depends on Examples Under Mars delay
1. Fully synchronous Instant back-and-forth Phone and video calls, live multiplayer games, live banter Breaks completely
2. Shared moment Experiencing the same event at the same time Live sports, concerts, watch parties, live streams, New Year's countdowns Breaks; the moment is gone before it arrives
3. Turn-based Ordered exchange, but each turn can wait Text chat, turn-based games, collaborative documents Works, but becomes very slow (Tables 3–4)
4. Self-contained Nothing from the other person Letters, recorded videos, books, podcasts, photo albums Unaffected

Table 6. Taxonomy of media by synchrony dependence.

The pattern is uncomfortable. The experiences that feel most like being together, levels 1 and 2, are exactly the ones that fail first, while the ones that survive, at level 4, are the ones that feel most like being apart. That tension runs through the rest of the paper.

The taxonomy also hints at what latency-native design has to do: take the experiences people value at levels 1 and 2 and rebuild them to work at levels 3 and 4, without losing the feeling of togetherness. A watch party can be rebuilt around a shared content timeline that does not require watching at the same time (Section 5.2), and a live game around ghosts and turns (Section 5.5). Whether the rebuilt versions still feel shared is a question for the human study in Appendix E; Chapters 6 and 7 test the opportunity side of it in simulation.

4.8 What the model predicts

The model leads to four predictions, which become the simulation hypotheses S1–S4 (Chapter 6) and the human-study hypotheses H1–H4 (Appendix E):

  1. A cliff rather than a slope (H1). Because Mars delay sits thousands of times beyond conversational tolerance (Table 5), the sense of togetherness that real-time designs provide should not fade gradually. It should collapse once delay reaches minutes.
  2. Design can recover connection (H2). Because the binding limit is shared time rather than raw delay (Table 4), designs that let people share experiences asynchronously should preserve more connection than designs that try to stay live.
  3. Frustration follows mismatch (H3). Real-time designs promise an immediacy they cannot deliver, so frustration should climb faster with delay for them than for latency-native designs.
  4. Sharing anchored to content works best (H4). Strategies that tie sharing to content rather than to the clock, such as asynchronous co-watching, escape both delay and schedule drift, so they should recover the most connection.

The model cannot say how strong these effects will be, or whether people will actually feel connected through latency-native designs. Chapters 6 and 7 test the predictions in simulation; measuring how people experience the designs is left to the human study described in Appendix E.

5. Latency-Native Design Strategies

Chapter 4 showed that three things limit interplanetary connection together: physical delay, mismatched schedules and periodic blackouts. A latency-native design accepts all three as permanent. Instead of asking how to make an experience feel instant, it asks what can still be shared when the other person will never be there at the same moment?

In this chapter I first set out the goals that any such design should meet, then describe four strategies, each aimed at a level of the taxonomy that breaks under delay. For each one I explain how it works, walk through what using it would be like, and note the main design choices, the existing evidence and the risks. The chapter ends with a comparison.

5.1 Design goals

The model and the research reviewed so far suggest five goals:

  1. Share experiences, not just messages. Messages on their own recreate letters. The aim is to recreate the feeling of doing something together.
  2. Work outside overlapping windows. Schedules overlap only about a third of the time (Table 4), so a design has to be useful even when the two people are never free at once.
  3. Spend scarce turns wisely. When only a few exchanges are possible each day, each one should carry as much as it can.
  4. Be honest about time. People should always know how old the thing in front of them is, and when a reply could arrive.
  5. Degrade gracefully. The design should keep working during blackouts, at maximum delay and when one person drops out for days.

5.2 Strategy 1: Asynchronous co-watching

A watch party or a live game matters because everyone reacts to the same moment together, and under delay that moment is over before it arrives. Asynchronous co-watching rebuilds this level-2 experience by anchoring every reaction to the content timeline instead of the clock. When someone on Earth laughs, gasps or comments at minute 12:04 of a film or a game broadcast, the system records the reaction (a short voice clip, a video of their face, an emoji or a line of text) and stamps it with the content time 12:04. When the settler watches later, that reaction appears at exactly 12:04, as if the person were sitting next to her. Her own reactions are stamped the same way and travel back to Earth, where her family can replay the game with her reactions in place. The content itself becomes the shared clock.

Return to the championship game from Chapter 1. On Saturday evening in Georgia, the settler's family watches with the co-watching app open, and it quietly records their reactions. The stream and the reaction track travel to Mars, where she watches during her own evening, eleven hours later by Earth's clock. Ninety seconds from the end, her mother's face appears in the corner of the screen with her hands over her mouth, and her cousin can be heard yelling. When her brother scores, every family member's reaction plays at the instant she sees the shot. She cheers, and her cheer is stamped to that second. The next day her family rewatches the last minute and hears her at exactly the right moment.

Several design choices decide whether this works. Spoilers are the biggest threat, so the interface has to hide scores, notifications and family chat about the content until the viewer reaches that point, perhaps with a temporary spoiler shield over her other feeds. Reactions should carry face and voice, not just text, in line with media richness theory [15] and the Mars-500 finding that video messages were the channel crews valued most [3]. Too many reactions clutter the screen and too few feel empty, so viewers should be able to choose whose reactions they see. And reactions have to flow in both directions, so that each side feels the other's presence.

Time-anchored comments already exist on some video platforms, and the popularity of reaction videos suggests people enjoy watching others respond to something they are watching. Those reactions, however, come from strangers or crowds. Co-watching with one known person's reactions has not been tested. The obvious risks are that spoilers prove hard to block in a connected world, and that for some people watching alone with recorded reactions may underline the absence rather than soften it.

5.3 Strategy 2: Predictive avatars

Live conversation depends on replies arriving within about 200 milliseconds [14], while at Mars distances every reply takes at least six minutes and usually far longer. Predictive avatars try to rebuild this level-1 experience with a local language model. While a real reply is in transit, the model writes a provisional one in the style of the other person, based on past messages that person has agreed to share. The provisional reply is unmistakably marked, with a faded colour, a different typeface and the word "predicted." When the real reply arrives it replaces the prediction, and the interface briefly shows whether the guess was right. It is the conversational version of client-side prediction in games [18]: guess first, correct later.

Suppose the settler writes to a friend on Earth: "Did you end up taking the job in Atlanta?" Within seconds a faded reply appears: "Predicted: Yes! Starting next month, I'm nervous though." Knowing it is a guess, she drafts a follow-up. Twenty-eight minutes later the real reply arrives: "Not yet, still deciding, they want an answer Friday." The prediction disappears, a small marker shows it was wrong, and her draft is flagged so she can revise it before sending.

The design questions here are mostly about honesty and control. A prediction must never be mistaken for a real message, either when it is read or later in the history. Predictions might be limited to low-stakes topics and switched off for emotional, medical, financial or relationship matters. The person being modelled must agree to it, be able to see what was predicted in their name, and be able to turn it off. Replies written in response to a prediction should be held for review rather than sent automatically, so that conversations are not built on guesses.

AI-suggested replies are already common in email and messaging, and research on AI-mediated communication shows that such tools can change how people present themselves and how far they trust what they read [21]. No one has tested person-specific prediction under minutes of delay. This is the most ethically sensitive strategy in the paper (Chapter 8): predictions could mislead people, comfort them with false information, crowd out real contact or be used to manipulate. I include it because the technology is now good enough that someone will probably build it, and its effects are better studied before that happens than after.

5.4 Strategy 3: Batched conversation

Chapter 4 showed that with realistic availability, interplanetary conversation runs at about one exchange a day. Quick one-line messages such as "lol," "wait what?" and "ok" waste those rare turns. Batched conversation reshapes level-3 messaging so that each turn carries more. The interface organizes a conversation into topic threads rather than a single timeline, reminds the sender which threads have unanswered questions before they hit send, and supports branching answers, in which the sender anticipates a likely follow-up ("if you mean the job, then…; if you mean the apartment, then…"). It encourages voice notes and short videos, and it can offer gentle prompts such as "Your sister asked three questions you haven't answered yet."

The settler opens her family thread once a day after her shift. Instead of a long scroll of fragments, she sees four threads: her brother's game, her mother's recovery from surgery, her cousin's wedding plans and a running joke. Each shows what is new and what is waiting for her. She records one six-minute video that answers all four, adding a note on the wedding thread: "If the venue is the lake one, I vote yes; if it's the hotel, call me back on this one."

Threading by topic keeps slow conversations coherent, and tracking open questions keeps anything from getting lost across days. The prompts have to stay optional, because batching should feel like help rather than homework. The strategy draws on Walther's observation that asynchronous media give people time to compose more thoughtful messages [16] and on the Mars-500 finding that video was especially valued during delay [3]. Its main risks are that long batched messages may overwhelm their recipients, and that some of the warmth of conversation lives in exactly the small, quick exchanges that batching discourages.

5.5 Strategy 4: Ghost multiplayer

Playing games together is one of the most common ways friends spend time, and real-time multiplayer is impossible at minutes of delay. Ghost multiplayer rebuilds this level-1 experience by having players interact with recordings of each other's play. In a racing game, the settler races her friend's best recorded lap and sends her own run back. In a puzzle or strategy game, both players tackle the same challenge and the game compares their approaches. In a cooperative game, they build or explore a shared world in turns, each leaving things for the other to find. Results accumulate into a running rivalry, with leaderboards, rematches and streaks, so the relationship carries on across weeks.

The settler and her best friend from high school keep exactly such a rivalry going in a racing game. Every few days a new ghost arrives from Earth with a short voice clip, "Beat that, Mars girl," and she races it until she wins, records a smug reply and sends her run back. Their all-time record sits at the top of the screen: 47–44.

For this to feel social, the ghost has to feel like a person, with a name, voice clips and small personal touches, and each match has to be part of a longer story. The games themselves need to be designed for asynchronous play from the start, rather than being real-time games with delay bolted on. Ghost racing and turn-based mobile games already show that asynchronous play can be engaging at scale [18]. Whether it feels social with a known person, rather than simply competitive, has not been tested, and in cooperative games, where real-time coordination is most of the fun, playing against a recording may feel a lot like playing alone.

5.6 Comparing the strategies

Strategy Rebuilds What becomes the shared element Works outside overlapping windows? Main risk
Asynchronous co-watching Live watch parties, live sports (level 2) The content timeline Yes Spoilers; may highlight absence
Predictive avatars Live conversation (level 1) A continuous conversational flow Partly Deception and loss of trust
Batched conversation Rapid chat (level 3) Depth of a long conversation Yes Effort and overload
Ghost multiplayer Real-time multiplayer (level 1) Competition and cooperation over time Yes Feeling of playing alone

Table 7. The four latency-native strategies.

Three of the four strategies work fully outside overlapping windows, which Chapter 4 identified as the binding constraint. Predictive avatars are the exception, since they help mainly while both people are actively talking. That is one reason I expect strategies anchored to content, such as co-watching, to recover more connection than predictive ones.

6. Simulation Methodology

The analytic model in Chapter 4 describes average limits. It cannot show how people with real, untidy schedules move through conversations, events and games over months, or how the design strategies change that. To get at those questions I built an agent-based, discrete-event simulator, which I call the Latency-Native Media Simulator (LNMS), and used it to run controlled experiments on simulated pairs of people.

It is worth being clear about what a simulation can and cannot tell us. It measures communication opportunity: how quickly conversations can finish, how many moments can be shared and how often people can play together. It does not measure how connected anyone feels. That question needs real participants, and Appendix E describes a study designed to answer it. I keep the distinction in view throughout the results.

6.1 The simulated pair

Each run simulates two people for 120 days, one on Earth and one off-Earth (whom I call the partner). The first 14 days are treated as a warm-up and left out of every measurement, which leaves 106 measured days.

Each person has three free windows a day on their own clock: half an hour in the morning, half an hour at lunch and four hours in the evening. On any given day, each window is independently lost to other commitments with probability 0.2. The Earth person's day is 24 hours long. A partner on Mars lives on Mars time, so their day is one sol, 24 hours 39 minutes 35 seconds, and their windows drift against Earth's by about 40 minutes a day. The starting offset between the two clocks is randomized for every run.

Every message, reaction or game move reaches the other person after a one-way delay D. During a solar-conjunction blackout, items queue until the link comes back and then travel with the normal delay. The simulator itself is an event-driven Python program: events such as a new topic, the start of a free window, a message arriving or a reply being written are kept in a time-ordered queue and processed in sequence, and a person can act only during their own free windows.

6.2 Activities and designs

Every run includes the three activities from Chapter 5, each under one of two designs.

Conversation. Each person starts new topics at random, two a day on average. A topic needs several back-and-forth turns to resolve, five extra turns on average, drawn from a geometric distribution. When a person is free and has topics waiting for their reply, they answer after a short reading-and-writing time with a median of 1.5 minutes. Under the baseline design, which reflects ordinary real-time habits, each waiting topic gets addressed in a given session with probability 0.75, so some are overlooked until later, and a quarter of all turns are spent on clarification ("wait, what do you mean?") that does not move the topic forward. Under the latency-native design, batched conversation (Section 5.4), open-question tracking means 97% of waiting topics are addressed each session, only 10% of turns go to clarification, and a quarter of turns are branching answers that settle two turns at once.

Shared events. Events on the Earth side, such as a game or a show, happen twice a week on average, start between 19:00 and 20:30 Earth time and last two hours. In the baseline design (a live stream plus live chat), a partner who is free for the whole event when the stream arrives watches it live and sees Earth reactions in step with the picture, but their own reactions reach Earth too late to be shared unless the one-way delay is under 5 seconds. If they are not free, they watch later and alone, and each Earth message that arrives in the meantime has a 30% chance of giving away the result. In the latency-native design (asynchronous co-watching, Section 5.2), the partner still watches live when possible and otherwise at the next window with enough time, within 72 hours. Earth reactions are anchored to the video, so they always appear at the right moment, and a spoiler shield cuts the chance of a leak to 3% per message. The partner's reactions travel back, and the Earth side replays them with probability 0.6 within 48 hours, which makes the sharing two-way.

Play. I count three forms. Real-time game sessions require both people to be free together for at least 30 minutes and a one-way delay under 0.15 seconds. Turn-based games of 20 moves are played continuously over the message link under both designs. Ghost matches, which exist only in the latency-native design (Section 5.5), happen when a person who has received a new recorded run plays against it in a free window, with probability 0.7, and sends their own run back.

I left predictive avatars (Section 5.3) out of the simulation. Their value depends almost entirely on whether people trust and accept machine-written replies, and a behavioural simulation has no honest way to represent that.

6.3 Parameters

Every behavioural parameter is an assumption, chosen to be plausible rather than measured. Table 8 lists them, and Section 7.6 tests how the results change when each one is halved or raised by half.

Chance a window is lost 0.20 same Assumption

Turns spent on clarification 25% 10% Assumed effect of richer, context-full messages [15], [16]

Table 8. Simulation parameters.

I ran seven fixed conditions and one in which delay changes over time (Table 9). Two of the fixed conditions are ablations: each switches on only one of the two Mars effects, which makes it possible to see how much each contributes on its own.
