6.6 Hypotheses

The predictions in Section 4.8 translate into four hypotheses for the simulation:

  • S1. Under real-time habits, Mars conditions sharply reduce shared events and lengthen conversations compared with Earth.
  • S2. At every Mars delay, latency-native designs shorten conversations and increase shared events compared with real-time habits.
  • S3. Schedule drift and delay each contribute substantially, and neither alone explains the Mars result.
  • S4. The advantage of latency-native designs is larger on Mars than on Earth.

6.7 Procedure and statistics

For each fixed condition and design I simulated 200 independent pairs, 2,800 runs in all. Each pair used the same random seed under both designs (common random numbers), so every comparison is between the same simulated people with the same schedules, and only the design differs. For each outcome I report the mean across pairs with a 95% confidence interval, along with the paired difference between designs. The full-cycle condition used 20 pairs per design, each run for 794 days.

6.8 Validation

To check the simulator's timing logic, I ran it in a stripped-down setting where the analytic model of Section 4.2 holds exactly: both people always available, nothing overlooked and no clarifications. In that setting each turn should take D + T minutes. Table 11 compares the two.

One-way delay D Simulated minutes per turn Analytic D + T Difference
0 min 1.69 1.80 −5.8%
3.2 min 4.83 5.00 −3.4%
13.9 min 15.98 15.70 +1.8%
22.3 min 24.60 24.10 +2.1%

Table 11. Simulator compared with the analytic model (40 runs of 200 days per row; T is the mean reply time, 1.8 minutes).

The simulator agrees with the analytic model to within 6% at every delay. The small differences come from topics that are still open when a run ends and from replies to several topics being written together.

6.9 Reproducibility

The simulator (sim.py), the experiment runner (experiments.py), the validation script (validate.py), the figure script (figures.py) and all raw results are included as supplementary material. Running python3 experiments.py 200 reproduces every number in Chapter 7.

7. Results

All of the results below come from the simulator described in Chapter 6, with 200 simulated pairs per condition and design, each measured over 106 days. Values are means across pairs, and ranges in brackets are 95% confidence intervals. With 200 pairs the intervals are mostly narrow, so differences that look large in the figures are also statistically clear. The more important question is whether they depend on my assumptions, which Section 7.6 takes up.

7.1 Conversation

Figure 4 and Table 12 show how long it takes to resolve a conversation topic.

Condition Baseline median (h) Latency-native median (h) Speed-up Baseline 90th percentile (h) Latency-native 90th percentile (h)
Earth (same clock) 6.5 5.0 1.31× 22.3 17.8
Moon (1.3 s) 6.5 5.0 1.31× 22.3 17.9
Drift only (0 delay) 19.7 13.1 1.50× 61.7 39.5
Delay only (13.9 min) 19.0 11.8 1.61× 53.7 34.8
Mars near (3.2 min) 28.0 15.5 1.80× 84.6 45.7
Mars average (13.9 min) 42.1 21.0 2.01× 122.1 61.1
Mars far (22.3 min) 44.5 21.9 2.03× 125.8 63.2

Table 12. Time to resolve a conversation topic.

Under ordinary real-time habits, a typical topic between two people in the same time zone on Earth is resolved in about 6.5 hours. At the average Mars delay, the same kind of topic takes 42 hours, close to two days, and one topic in ten takes more than five days (122 hours). That is about 6.5 times slower than on Earth. The Moon, at 1.3 seconds, makes no measurable difference to messaging.

Latency-native messaging cuts Mars conversation time roughly in half. At the average delay the median falls from 42.1 to 21.0 hours, a paired reduction of 21.2 hours [20.8, 21.5], and the improvement held for every one of the 200 simulated pairs at every Mars delay. The slowest topics gain the most in absolute terms, with the 90th percentile dropping from 122 to 61 hours.

The benefit also grows with distance. On Earth, latency-native messaging is 1.31 times faster; at the average and far Mars delays it is about twice as fast. Habits that are a minor convenience at home become a substantial advantage between planets.

7.2 Delay and drift compound

The two ablation conditions separate the two Mars effects. Schedule drift alone raises the baseline median from 6.5 to 19.7 hours, and a 13.9-minute delay alone raises it to 19.0 hours, so each roughly triples conversation time by itself. If the two simply added together, the combined result would be about 32 hours (6.5 + 13.2 + 12.5). The actual Mars-average figure is 42.1 hours, around 30% worse than additive. The effects compound: delay eats into whatever free time overlaps, and drift makes overlapping free time rare in the first place.

The same interaction explains a row in Table 12 that might otherwise look odd. Mars at its closest (3.2 minutes, with drift) is slower than a 13.9-minute delay without drift. Across the range I modelled, mismatched days matter more than the speed of light.

7.3 Shared events

Condition Design Shared both ways Shared one way Watched later, alone Spoiled before watching
Earth (same clock) Baseline 81% 81% 2% 17%
Earth (same clock) Latency-native 89% 94% 0% 6%
Mars average Baseline 0% 7% 65% 27%
Mars average Latency-native 57% 96% 0% 3%

Table 13. What happened to Earth-side events. "Shared one way" includes events also shared both ways. Missed events (about 1%) are not shown.

With real-time habits, shared events effectively vanish on Mars. At every Mars delay, 0% of events were shared in both directions, because the partner's reactions always reach Earth minutes after the moment has passed. Only 7% were shared even one way, in the few cases where the partner happened to be free just as the stream arrived. Most events were watched later and alone (65%), and more than a quarter (27%) were spoiled before the partner could watch them.

Co-watching changes the picture. 96% of events were shared one way and 57% both ways (a paired gain of 57 percentage points [56, 59]), and the figures barely moved across the Mars delays. The two-way share is lower because it depends on the Earth side choosing to replay the partner's reactions, which Section 7.6 examines. Spoilers fell from 27% to 3%.

7.4 Play

Real-time games, which need a one-way delay under 0.15 seconds, are possible only on Earth, where the pair manages about 13.5 sessions a week; on the Moon and on Mars the number is zero. Turn-based games survive but slow down sharply, from about 37.7 completed games a week on Earth to 2.0 at the average Mars delay. Ghost matches hardly notice the delay at all: about 12 a week on Earth and 14.7 at the average Mars delay. They even run slightly higher under drift, because when two people's free windows are spread across the day, a fresh recording is more often waiting whenever one of them sits down to play.

7.5 Over a full Earth–Mars cycle

Over a full 26-month cycle with the delay changing every day, the results match the fixed conditions closely: a median of 41.1 hours under real-time habits against 20.5 hours with latency-native messaging, and 0% against 57% of events shared both ways. Conversation time creeps upward as delay grows toward conjunction, but the blackout overwhelms everything else. Topics caught in it take a median of about 200–220 hours to resolve under either design. No design can overcome a link that is down, which reinforces the argument in Section 4.5 for helping people prepare messages and content before a blackout begins.

7.6 Sensitivity analysis

Because the behavioural parameters are assumptions, I re-ran the Mars-average condition with each one set to half and to one and a half times its default (probabilities capped at 0.99), leaving the others at default, with 100 pairs per setting.

The sharing result holds up well. The gain in two-way sharing stays between 56 and 60 percentage points under every change but one: how often the Earth side replays the partner's reactions. That single assumption moves the gain anywhere from 30 to 86 points, so the two-way figure is best read as a large gain whose exact size depends on habits at the Earth end.

The conversation result is more fragile. Under most changes the speed-up stays between 1.7× and 2.4×, but it is very sensitive to two parameters. One is how often waiting topics get overlooked under baseline habits, which moves the speed-up from 1.4× to 4.4×. The other matters more: how well open-question tracking actually works under the latency-native design. If tracking addresses only 49% of waiting topics, which is worse than baseline habits, latency-native messaging becomes slower than the baseline (0.87×). Batched conversation, in other words, helps only if its question tracking really does help people answer more of what is waiting for them. That is the most important thing for any real-world test to measure.

7.7 Summary against the hypotheses

Hypothesis Result Evidence
S1: Mars sharply reduces shared events and lengthens conversations under real-time habits Supported Conversations 6.5× slower; two-way shared events 81% → 0%
S2: Latency-native designs help at every Mars delay Supported, conditionally 1.8–2.0× faster conversations and +57 pp two-way sharing in all 200 pairs; conversation benefit reverses if question tracking performs worse than baseline habits
S3: Delay and drift both contribute substantially Supported Each alone roughly triples conversation time; together they compound to 6.5×
S4: The advantage is larger on Mars than on Earth Supported Speed-up 1.31× on Earth vs ~2.0× on Mars; sharing gain +8 pp on Earth vs +57 pp on Mars

Table 14. Results against the simulation hypotheses.

8. Discussion

This chapter steps back from the details. I first argue that interplanetary delay creates a new medium rather than a degraded version of an old one (8.1). I then consider what the simulation shows and how far it can be trusted (8.2), propose design principles (8.3), take up the ethics of predictive avatars and the broader question of what counts as real connection (8.4 and 8.5), and close with limitations and future work (8.6 and 8.7).

8.1 A different medium, not a worse one

The model in Chapter 4 makes one point hard to escape. With a synchrony gap in the thousands, talking to someone on Mars is not a slow phone call. Once schedules and drifting days are counted, it behaves much more like an exchange of letters, at roughly one round a day. Stretching real-time media across that gap gives people the worst of both worlds: tools that promise instant contact and then make them wait, every single time.

History offers some comfort. Nobody treated letters as broken conversations; they developed their own forms, rituals and kinds of intimacy. Walther's hyperpersonal model even suggests that slow, carefully composed communication can sometimes produce stronger impressions of closeness than fast exchange [16]. The opportunity is to give interplanetary communication forms of its own on purpose, rather than leaving it as a frustrating imitation of real-time media.

8.2 What the simulation shows, and how far to trust it

The simulation supports the central argument in three ways. It confirms that real-time habits fail on Mars in just the places the taxonomy predicted: real-time games disappear, two-way shared moments drop to zero, and conversations stretch over days (Chapter 7). It shows that latency-native designs win back much of what is lost, with conversations about twice as fast and most events shared again. And it brings out something the analytic model only hinted at, which is that schedule drift does as much damage as the speed of light, and the two compound. A settlement that kept Earth time would avoid drift entirely, but only by living out of step with the Martian day, and that trade-off deserves study in its own right.

Three cautions apply. First, the results describe opportunity, not experience: a topic resolved twice as fast, or an event "shared both ways," does not prove that anyone felt closer. Second, the behavioural parameters are assumptions. The sensitivity analysis suggests the sharing result is robust, while the conversation result depends on whether question tracking really helps people answer more of what is waiting. Third, the simulated people are simple. They do not tire of long delays, change their habits or favour some relationships over others. Each caution points straight at something a human study needs to test (Appendix E), and Table 15 sets out how such a study could confirm or overturn the simulation's findings.

If the human study finds… It would mean… Implication for design
Co-watching increases felt connection, as the simulation's opportunity gains suggest Opportunity translates into experience Invest in content-anchored media now; test on the Moon first
More opportunity but no gain in felt connection Recorded presence is not enough Rethink what makes reactions feel live
Question tracking does not raise how many topics people answer The conversation benefit in the simulation does not materialize Redesign or drop batched conversation
Connection falls over a week despite the tools Short-term effects fade Long-duration testing in analog habitats is essential

Table 15. How a human study could confirm or overturn the simulation results.

8.3 Design principles for latency-native media

Drawing on the model, the strategies and the simulation, I propose six working principles. They are hypotheses about good design, to be confirmed, revised or discarded as evidence comes in.

  1. Anchor to content, not the clock. Shared experiences should be synchronized to a common timeline, such as a video, a game or a story, rather than to real time. That way they escape both delay and schedule drift.
  2. Make every turn count. When turns are scarce, interfaces should help people put more into each one: more topics, more context and richer media.
  3. Make time visible. People cope better with waiting they can see and understand. Interfaces should show how old incoming content is, when a sent message will arrive and the earliest moment a reply could come back.
  4. Keep the person and the prediction separate. Anything a machine generates in place of a person must be clearly and permanently marked, and replaced by the real thing when it arrives.
  5. Design for drift and darkness. Systems should adjust to changing delay, to schedules that slide apart and to blackouts during solar conjunction, for example by letting people prepare messages and content in advance.
  6. Protect the rituals. Birthdays, holidays, anniversaries and big games matter because they are shared. Latency-native media should give these moments special support, such as timing a recorded greeting to arrive at the right local hour on Mars.

8.4 The ethics of predictive avatars

Predictive avatars are the most powerful strategy in this paper and also the most dangerous. Four risks stand out.

  • Deception. Even with clear labels, people may come to remember predicted words as things the other person really said.
  • Substitution. An always-available prediction could gradually displace the slow, real reply, so that people feel connected while in fact talking less.
  • Misrepresentation. A model can put words in someone's mouth that they would never say, including on topics where mistakes matter, such as health, money or relationships.
  • Manipulation and misuse. A system that can imitate a person could be used by others to influence, impersonate or deceive.

These concerns echo the questions that research on AI-mediated communication has raised about self-presentation, trust and the line between what a person says and what a machine says for them [21]. Before any real deployment, predictive avatars would need at least explicit consent from the person being modelled, permanent and unmistakable labelling, limits on topics and on how far a prediction can run ahead, and a way for the modelled person to review and correct what was said in their name. Because the simulation cannot model trust, the planned human study (Appendix E) measures trust and discomfort directly, so that these risks are tested rather than assumed.

8.5 What counts as real connection?

Underneath all four strategies sits a harder question. If a settler laughs at her mother's recorded reaction eleven hours after it happened, are they sharing a moment, or is she watching a recording of someone else's? My measures can say whether people feel together, but not whether that feeling amounts to being together. Philosophers and communication researchers have argued about versions of this question for letters, phone calls and social media, and I do not try to settle it here. I would only point out that people throughout history have found real meaning in delayed communication, and that the realistic alternative for a settler is not instant contact but no shared experience at all.

8.6 Limitations

  • Opportunity is not connection. The simulation counts what is possible, not what people feel. This is the most important limitation, and the reason the human study in Appendix E matters.
  • Assumed behaviour. All behavioural parameters (Table 8) are assumptions, not measurements. The sensitivity analysis (Section 7.6) shows which ones matter most: how well question tracking works and how often the Earth side replays reactions.
  • Simple agents. Simulated people follow fixed schedules and probabilities, whereas real people adapt, get tired, set priorities and sometimes stop trying.
  • One relationship at a time. Each run models a single pair, while real settlers will juggle many relationships and a community around them.
  • Predictive avatars not simulated. Their value depends on trust and acceptance, which a behavioural simulation cannot represent honestly.
  • A simplified link. The model ignores processing delay, bandwidth limits and partial outages, and it relies on a two-dimensional orbital model accurate to about ±0.3 minutes (Appendix A).

8.7 Future work

The obvious next step is a study with human participants to test whether the simulation's gains in opportunity turn into gains in felt connection. Appendix E describes a ready-to-run design, with instruments in Appendices B to D. Beyond that, I see three directions. The simulator could be calibrated against real behavioural data, for instance message timing from people living with large time-zone differences, so that assumed parameters give way to measured ones. It could be extended from pairs to whole communities, to study how a settlement shares news, culture and celebrations with Earth. And it could compare timekeeping policies, such as Mars time, Earth time or hybrid schedules, since Chapter 7 shows that drift alone roughly triples conversation time.

9. Future Applications

Mars motivates latency-native media, but their uses begin much sooner and much closer to home. I go through them roughly in the order they could matter, and then propose a roadmap.

9.1 Earth, today

Plenty of people already live with high, unreliable or effective latency. Researchers at Antarctic stations, crews on submarines and long-haul ships, and workers at remote mines and offshore platforms often have limited, intermittent connections. Billions of people still depend on slow or unreliable internet, where real-time video is impractical but asynchronous media work fine. After hurricanes and earthquakes, networks are often degraded for days, exactly when families most need to stay in touch. And military families during deployment, shift workers and families spread across many time zones face the same scheduling problem modelled in Chapter 4, even on fast networks; for them, the delay comes from the clock rather than the speed of light. For all of these groups, co-watching and batched conversation in particular could be built and tested today.

9.2 The Moon, in the late 2020s and 2030s

NASA's Moon to Mars Architecture presents the Artemis program as preparation for crewed Mars missions [12]. Crews on the Moon will face delays of seconds, perhaps up to 10 seconds once processing is included [1], which is enough to make conversation awkward (a synchrony gap of roughly 6 to 50, Chapter 4). That makes the Moon the natural place to test latency-native tools with real crews under real delay before anyone needs them on Mars.

9.3 Mars missions, late 2030s and beyond

Outside estimates put the first crewed Mars mission in the late 2030s or early 2040s, with a round trip of about 500 days [13]. Mars-500 showed that private contact with the outside world becomes central to psychological support once real-time communication is gone [4]. Latency-native tools could become a standard part of the support available to these crews, alongside the operational autonomy tools that agencies are already developing [6].

9.4 Permanent settlements and interplanetary culture

In the longer run, a permanent settlement will want to take part in Earth's culture, not just receive it late. That raises design questions on a much larger scale. Sports broadcasts and live events could be designed with audiences on two planets in mind, for instance with pinned reactions from fans on both. Games could be built from the start for asynchronous play across worlds, with long-running interplanetary leagues. News and politics will have to serve citizens who always learn things minutes or hours after everyone else. And over generations, a population separated by permanent delay may develop its own language, humour and norms. Latency-native media will help decide whether Earth and Mars remain one culture or slowly become two.

9.5 Responsible AI

The questions raised by predictive avatars, about when a machine may speak for a person, how it must be labelled and who controls it, will matter on Earth long before anyone settles Mars. The interplanetary case is simply a clean and extreme version of a problem that AI-mediated communication [21] already poses.

9.6 A roadmap

Phase Timeframe Setting Goal
1. Simulation study (this paper), then lab study 2026–2027 University lab (Study 1) Test whether latency-native designs recover connection under simulated delay
2. Field study 2027 Daily life (Study 2) Test whether effects hold over a week of true delay and drifting schedules
3. Earth deployments 2028–2030 Polar stations, ships, deployed families Test with people who already live with real latency
4. Analog habitats 2028–2032 HERA or similar long-duration analogs Test over weeks to months in isolation
5. Lunar operations 2030s Artemis-era crews Refine tools under real, small delays
6. Mars readiness late 2030s+ First crewed Mars missions Ship mature latency-native tools as part of crew support

Table 16. Proposed research roadmap. Later timeframes depend on agency mission schedules and are indicative only.

10. Conclusion

Humanity is preparing to send people to live on other worlds, and most of the planning, quite rightly, is about keeping them alive. My argument in this paper is that keeping them connected deserves the same early attention.

Interplanetary delay is set by physics and cannot be engineered away. At Mars distances it puts people roughly a thousand to seven thousand times beyond the limits of natural conversation, and once schedules and drifting days are counted, a settler may get only a few live exchanges a day with the people she loves, against hundreds for families on Earth. The experiences that make us feel most together, conversation, shared moments and play, are exactly the ones that break first.

In response I have offered a quantitative model that measures the problem, a taxonomy that shows which experiences fail and why, and four latency-native design strategies that rebuild shared experience around delay instead of fighting it. A simulation of 2,800 runs suggests that these strategies roughly halve conversation time on Mars and restore most shared moments, and I have set out how to test them with real people. I have also proposed design principles and named the ethical risks, above all those of machines that speak for people.

The broader claim is a simple one. The media of an interplanetary civilization will not be today's media slowed down. They will be something new, and the time to start designing them is before the first settlers need them. The settler watching her brother's championship game 22 minutes late does not need a faster radio. She needs a better way to be there.

Appendix A. Orbital Delay Model

This appendix documents how Figure 1 and the delay values in Chapters 2 and 4 were computed, so that the results can be reproduced.

A.1 Orbital elements

I use the J2000 mean orbital elements for Earth and Mars, measured from the J2000 epoch (12:00 UTC, 1 January 2000).

Element Earth Mars
Semi-major axis a (AU) 1.00000261 1.52371034
Eccentricity e 0.01671123 0.09339410
Longitude of perihelion ϖ (degrees) 102.93768 −23.94363
Mean longitude at epoch L₀ (degrees) 100.46457 −4.55343
Mean motion n (degrees per day) 0.98560028 0.52402068

Table A1. Mean orbital elements used in the model.

A.2 Algorithm

For each day t from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2035:

  1. Compute days since epoch, d = t − J2000.
  2. For each planet, compute the mean longitude L = L₀ + n·d and the mean anomaly M = L − ϖ.
  3. Solve Kepler's equation for the eccentric anomaly E by Newton's method (30 iterations):
  1. Compute the position in the orbital plane, then rotate by ϖ into a shared heliocentric frame:
  1. Compute the Earth–Mars distance d in AU and convert to one-way delay: D (minutes) = d × 499.0048 / 60.

A.3 Simplifications

  • Two-dimensional. The model ignores Mars's 1.85° orbital inclination. This introduces an error of roughly ±0.3 minutes.
  • Mean elements. It uses fixed mean elements and ignores gravitational perturbations between planets, which shift positions slightly over a decade.
  • Light travel only. It ignores processing, relay and queuing delays (Chapter 2), so all values are lower bounds on real delay.

A.4 Validation

Quantity Model (2026–2035) Published reference
Minimum one-way delay 3.2 min (Sep 2035) About 3.5 min [1]
Maximum one-way delay 22.3 min (Aug 2034) Just over 22 min [1]
Synodic period ~26 months ~780 days (standard value)

Table A2. Model results compared with published values.

The model's minimum is slightly lower than ESA's figure because 2035 brings an unusually favourable perihelic opposition within the modelled decade. For mission-planning precision, the calculation should be repeated with a full ephemeris such as NASA JPL's Horizons system.

A.5 Code

The full Python script (about 30 lines using NumPy) is included in the supplementary materials alongside the figure files. The core of the position calculation is:

def position(d, a, e, varpi, L0, n):
    M = np.radians(L0 + n * d - varpi) % (2 * np.pi)
    E = M.copy()
    for _ in range(30):                       # Newton's method
        E -= (E - e * np.sin(E) - M) / (1 - e * np.cos(E))
    x, y = a * (np.cos(E) - e), a * np.sqrt(1 - e**2) * np.sin(E)
    w = np.radians(varpi)                     # rotate into shared frame
    return x*np.cos(w) - y*np.sin(w), x*np.sin(w) + y*np.cos(w)

Appendix B. Study Instruments

This appendix lists every questionnaire used in the studies. Established scales are described and cited rather than reproduced; their full item lists should be obtained from the original authors. Items written for this study are given in full.

B.1 Per-trial questionnaire (Study 1)

Completed by each participant after every trial, in about two minutes.

Part 1: Social presence. A short form of the Networked Minds Social Presence Inventory [9], rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Select two to three items from each of these subscales: co-presence, attentional allocation, perceived message understanding, and perceived affective and behavioral interdependence. Use the same items after every trial. Obtain the item wording from Biocca and Harms's published inventory.

Part 2: Workload. The NASA Task Load Index [23], rated 0–100 on six subscales: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort and frustration. Use the unweighted ("raw TLX") version to save time, and report the frustration subscale separately for H3.

Part 3: Quick check items (written for this study, 1–7 scale):

  1. During this activity, it felt like we were doing something together.
  2. I knew what my partner was thinking or feeling during this activity.
  3. I would choose to use this version again to stay in touch with this person.

B.2 Prediction trust items (Studies 1 and 2)

Completed after any trial or day in which predicted replies were switched on (1–7 scale, written for this study):

  1. I could always tell which replies were predicted and which were real.
  2. The predicted replies sounded like my partner.
  3. The predicted replies were usually correct about what my partner would say.
  4. Seeing predicted replies made me feel closer to my partner.
  5. I was uncomfortable with a computer writing replies in my partner's style.
  6. I was comfortable with a computer writing replies in my style for my partner to read.

One open question: Was there a moment when a predicted reply helped, or caused a problem? Please describe it.

B.3 Daily diary (Study 2)

Shown in the app each evening, in about two minutes.

Ratings (1–7):

  1. Today, I felt connected to my partner.
  2. Today, I felt frustrated by the delay.
  3. Today, I felt lonely.
  4. Today, my partner felt present in my day.

Tool use (check all that apply): co-watching · batched messages · voice or video messages · ghost game · predicted replies · none.

Open questions:

  • What was the most connected moment with your partner today?
  • What was the most frustrating or lonely moment?
  • Is there anything you wanted to share today but did not, because of the delay?

B.4 Relationship closeness (Studies 1 and 2)

The Inclusion of Other in the Self scale [22], a single item showing seven pairs of circles that overlap to increasing degrees. Participants choose the pair that best describes their relationship with their partner. Administered at the start of the first session and at the end of the last session (Study 1), and on day 0 and day 7 (Study 2).

B.5 Demographics

Age, gender (with an open option and "prefer not to say"), field of study, relationship to partner (friend, sibling, partner, other), years known, and typical frequency of contact before the study. Do not collect any information that is not used in analysis.

Appendix C. Interview Guides

Interviews are semi-structured: the interviewer covers each topic but follows the participant's lead, using follow-up prompts only where helpful. Each member of a pair is interviewed separately. Interviews are audio-recorded with consent and transcribed.

C.1 Study 1: end-of-session interview (about 10 minutes)

Opening

  1. In your own words, how did today's session feel overall?

Comparing versions

  1. Think about the two versions of today's activity. Which one made you feel more connected to your partner? What made the difference? - Prompt: Was there a specific moment you remember?
  2. How did the longer "Mars" delays change the experience? - Prompt: Did you find yourself doing anything differently while you waited?

Activity-specific questions

  1. (Shared viewing) When your partner's reactions appeared at the same point in the video, what was that like? Did it feel like watching together, or like watching a recording?
  2. (Conversation) Did you notice yourself writing differently under long delays? Did the topic threads or reminders help or get in the way?
  3. (Conversation, if predictions were on) What did you think of the predicted replies? Did they change how you felt about your partner's real replies?
  4. (Play) Playing against your partner's recorded run, did it feel like playing with them or playing alone?

Closing

  1. If you had to live far from this person for years with this kind of delay, which tools would you want, and what is missing?
  2. Is there anything else you would like to tell us?

C.2 Study 2: end-of-week interview (about 20 minutes)

The week overall

  1. Tell me about your week as the "Earth" or "Mars" partner. What stands out?
  2. How did your sense of connection to your partner change across the week? - Prompt: Was there a turning point, good or bad?

Living with delay and drift

  1. How did you handle the delay day to day? Did you develop any habits or routines?
  2. How did the shifting "available" windows affect you? - Prompt: Were there days when you never seemed to overlap? What did you do?
  3. Was there anything you wanted to share but did not, because of the delay or timing?

Tools

  1. Which tools did you use most, and why?
  2. Tell me about the shared event you co-watched. How did it compare with watching something together normally?
  3. (If used) How did you feel about predicted replies over the week? Did your view change?
  4. Which tools would you keep, and which would you drop?

The Mars rule

  1. How hard was it to avoid contacting your partner in other ways? Did you break the rule at any point? (Reassure the participant that honest answers are what matter and that there is no penalty.)

Closing

  1. Imagine your partner really were on Mars for five years. What would you most need from technology to stay close?
  2. Is there anything else you would like to tell us?

Appendix D. Study Protocol and IRB Preparation

Undergraduate researchers usually need a faculty member to serve as principal investigator on an IRB application. This checklist covers what to prepare before submitting. Check your institution's current IRB requirements and forms, since procedures and templates change.

D.1 Before submission

  • ☐ Find a faculty sponsor to act as principal investigator
  • ☐ Complete the required human-subjects research training (many universities use CITI training; confirm with the IRB office)
  • ☐ Decide whether the study likely qualifies as exempt or minimal-risk review, and confirm with the IRB office
  • ☐ Run the power analysis and fix the Study 1 sample size (Appendix E)

D.2 Documents to prepare

  • ☐ Research protocol: aims, design, procedures, risks and protections (adapt Appendix E)
  • ☐ Informed consent form for Study 1
  • ☐ Informed consent form for Study 2, including the Mars rule and the right to end it early
  • ☐ Separate consent for being modelled by the predictive reply feature
  • ☐ Recruitment materials: flyer, email and social media text
  • ☐ All instruments (Appendix B) and interview guides (Appendix C)
  • ☐ Data management plan: what is stored, where, for how long, and when content is deleted
  • ☐ Compensation plan and budget

D.3 Risks to address in the protocol

Risk Mitigation
Distress from reduced contact during Study 2 Mars rule is voluntary; participants may end it at any time for any reason; contact details for counselling services provided
Privacy of message content Content deleted after each session unless both partners consent; logs keep only timing, type and length
Discomfort with predictive replies Feature is optional; requires consent from the person modelled; either partner can switch it off
Relationship strain between partners Pairs choose to enrol together; either can withdraw without the other being told why
Data breach Encrypted storage on university systems; participant codes instead of names

Table D1. Main risks and mitigations.

D.4 Running the study

  • ☐ Pilot the simulator and full procedure with 2–3 pairs; fix problems; do not include pilot data in analysis
  • ☐ Pre-register hypotheses H1–H4 and the analysis plan (for example on OSF) before collecting main data
  • ☐ Run Study 1 sessions
  • ☐ Run Study 2
  • ☐ Transcribe interviews and complete thematic coding with a second coder
  • ☐ Analyze data and report the human-study results
  • ☐ Replace Figure E2 with measured results

Appendix E. Planned Human-Participant Validation Study

The simulation in this paper measures communication opportunity. The natural follow-up is a study with real people that tests whether more opportunity produces more felt connection. This appendix records a ready-to-run design so that the work can continue once a faculty sponsor and ethics approval are available (Appendix D). The instruments are in Appendix B and the interview guides in Appendix C.

E.1 Design overview

Study 1 (lab experiment). Pairs of friends, in separate rooms, use a web-based delay simulator for three activities (conversation, shared viewing, play), each in a standard and a latency-native version, at four delays: 0 s, 1.3 s, 4 min and 20 min. The two Mars delays are time-compressed by a factor of 10 so that each trial lasts about five minutes. Each pair completes three sessions of about 75 minutes, one per activity, with conditions in counterbalanced order. Target: about 24 pairs.

Study 2 (one-week field study). About 8–10 pairs use the latency-native tools in daily life for seven days, with a true delay of about 14 minutes and simulated Mars-sol schedule drift. Both partners agree not to contact each other by any other channel during the week (the "Mars rule"), which either may end at any time. Each evening, a two-minute diary records connection and frustration.

E.2 Hypotheses

  • H1. For standard designs, social presence drops sharply once delay reaches minutes.
  • H2. At 4 and 20 minutes, latency-native designs produce higher social presence than standard designs.
  • H3. Frustration rises with delay more steeply for standard designs.
  • H4. Shared viewing shows the largest gain from latency-native design, mirroring the simulation's largest effect (Chapter 7.3).

The simulation adds one more question with high priority: does question tracking actually increase how many waiting topics people answer? Section 7.6 showed that the conversation benefit depends on it.

E.3 Measures and analysis

Social presence (short form of the Networked Minds inventory [9]), NASA-TLX workload and frustration [23], closeness (IOS [22]), event logs and interviews. Analysis uses linear mixed-effects models with delay, design and their interaction as fixed effects and participant nested within pair as a random effect, with thematic analysis of interviews by two independent coders. Hypotheses and analysis should be pre-registered before data collection.
